reasons: The file holds type definitions only, so there is no behaviour to test here.
No test file was shown for this file.
Several fields are marked as absent on older runs, so older data is only partly described.

terms.meaning: a written description of what a piece of data must look like, including its field names and kinds.
a field that may be missing from a saved record, usually because older runs did not store it.
the check of whether a cited web page actually supports a fact's wording and numbers.
one of the main groups of drivers used to explain why projects succeed or struggle.
a specific driver inside a pillar, such as one named cause of success or failure.
the collection of recorded facts about each project that the analysis draws on.
a statement paired with the IDs of the sources or facts that back it.

used_by: artifacts/api-server/src/tools/lessons-learnt/recipe/synthesis.ts (uses several of these names; its import list is not shown)

sections.name: File setup, OutcomeLabel
sections.title: File header and outcome labels
sections.what: Explains where the contract comes from and defines the four outcome labels a project can carry: Delivered, Overran, Cautionary and In progress.
sections.why: The header says outcome is kept separate from the driver pillars, so a project's result is not used to prove its drivers.
sections.watch_out: The synthesis code uses these four names directly, and recipeResult.ts also allows Unassessed, so the two lists differ.

sections.name: VerificationStatus, RelevanceStatus, Stance
sections.title: Verification, relevance and stance labels
sections.what: Lists the allowed labels for how a fact matched its source (verified, partial, unverified, unreachable, unsourced), how relevant it is to its project, and whether a finding is a strength, risk, watch point or neutral.
sections.why: Each verification label has a comment explaining what happened when the source was checked.
sections.watch_out: A partial or unverified label does not prove a fact is false, only that the cited page did not carry enough of its wording.

sections.name: RecipeProject
sections.title: Project record fields
sections.what: Describes each project in the analysis: name, location, technology, parties, status, budgets, cost overrun, delay, key dates, its assigned outcome, and how much evidence it has.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed record shape keeps every project comparable.
sections.watch_out: Budgets are stored as numbers with a unit flag of M or raw, so a value read without its unit can be wrong by a large factor.

sections.name: RecipeFact
sections.title: Fact record fields
sections.what: Describes one piece of evidence: its statement, source address, publisher, verification result, relevance, the pillar and sub-driver it supports, and whether it was admitted or held out and why.
sections.why: Likely reason: each fact keeps its source and check result so every report claim can be traced back.
sections.watch_out: A fact supports a driver only when its admitted flag is true, so check that flag and the held reason before trusting its place in the report.

sections.name: RecipeFinding
sections.title: Finding record fields
sections.what: Describes a conclusion drawn about one project: its text, stance, confidence, the facts it is grounded on, and its pillar.
sections.why: Likely reason: findings separate the analysed conclusion from the raw evidence beneath it.
sections.watch_out: An empty grounded list means the finding names no supporting facts, so it should be read with caution.

sections.name: RecipeCommentary
sections.title: Commentary record fields
sections.what: Stores a named person's comment about a project, with their role, a paraphrase of what they said, and a link.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps interview or commentary material separate from documented facts.
sections.watch_out: The text is a paraphrase, not a verbatim quote, so it should not be presented as the person's exact words.

sections.name: MethodSource
sections.title: Source record for the method
sections.what: Records each outside source used to build the method: its channel, address, title, publisher, year, check date, whether it could be read, the captured passage, its tier and any reason it was excluded.
sections.why: The tier comment says it follows a research source policy, from official sources at tier 1 down to banned sources at tier 4.
sections.watch_out: The tier and excluded reason exist only on newer runs, so older saved results may not have them.

sections.name: MethodItem
sections.title: Method item record
sections.what: Describes one benchmark, framework or practice drawn from a source, with the source ID and the quote that supports it.
sections.why: Likely reason: each method item must cite a quote so the method can be checked.
sections.watch_out: The quote is stored as text, so if the source page changes later, the quote may no longer match what the page says.

sections.name: Methodology
sections.title: Methodology bundle
sections.what: Groups everything about how the research was done: the central argument, searches run, sources, accepted items, a count of rejected items, provider health and qualification notes.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeping these together lets the report show its own method.
sections.watch_out: Rejected items are stored only as a count, so the items themselves cannot be reviewed from this record.

sections.name: SubDriver
sections.title: Sub-driver record
sections.what: Describes one specific driver under a pillar: its ID, letter, text, the reason it matters, its keywords and the method items that back it.
sections.why: Likely reason: sub-drivers break a pillar into smaller parts that can each be tested against the evidence.
sections.watch_out: IDs such as P2.b are used as references, so renaming or reordering them can break links to older results.

sections.name: Pillar
sections.title: Pillar record
sections.what: Describes one main driver group: its ID, name, principle, categories, keywords, method support, a rubric for judging a project as success, mixed or challenge, and its sub-drivers.
sections.why: Likely reason: the rubric lets every project be judged against the same standard within a pillar.
sections.watch_out: Pillars are written fresh for each run, so an ID such as P1 may mean something different in another run.

sections.name: Framework, CellScore
sections.title: Framework and cell score
sections.what: Describes the full set of pillars for a run, a count of categories with any unclaimed ones listed, and the five possible scores a project can get in one pillar.
sections.why: Likely reason: the unclaimed list shows where the framework has gaps.
sections.watch_out: Facts in categories that no pillar claimed may not appear under any pillar in the report.

sections.name: Assessment
sections.title: Assessment grid
sections.what: Records how each project scored in each pillar, with the facts behind each score, plus per-pillar totals, sub-driver groupings, lists of good, caution and neutral items, and counts of facts that were not placed in any pillar.
sections.why: Likely reason: the grid is the basis for the assessment matrix view and the cross-project comparisons.
sections.watch_out: The strength and risk weights are stored as bare numbers with no unit, so read them only through the code that writes them.

sections.name: Discrimination, Cited
sections.title: Discrimination measure and cited text
sections.what: Measures whether a pillar tells delivered projects apart from troubled ones, giving an index from minus one to one and a label. Also defines the standard pairing of a claim with the sources that back it.
sections.why: Likely reason: a pillar that scores the same for both groups does not help explain outcomes, and the index shows that difference.
sections.watch_out: The index is left empty when either group has fewer than three projects, so a small sample shows as insufficient rather than as a result.

sections.name: SubProfile
sections.title: Sub-driver profile
sections.what: Summarises one sub-driver with its written profile, examples of projects that did well on it, and cautionary tales of projects that did badly.
sections.why: Likely reason: a sub-driver is easier to judge when shown next to real project examples.
sections.watch_out: Examples store project IDs and citations, so if a project is removed, these examples can point at nothing.

sections.name: PillarProfile
sections.title: Pillar profile
sections.what: Holds the written profile of one pillar: an overview, recommended practices, implications, and a profile for each of its sub-drivers.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps all the written text for a pillar in one place for the report.
sections.watch_out: Each part is a list of cited claims, and claims without a valid citation are expected to be removed earlier by the synthesis step.

sections.name: CaseSummary
sections.title: Project summary
sections.what: Holds a short summary of one project: a headline and a takeaway for each pillar, marked as success, challenge or mixed.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives a single project a compact summary that can sit on one page.
sections.watch_out: The direction values are fixed as success, challenge or mixed, which are different words from the outcome labels.

sections.name: Synthesis
sections.title: Whole-analysis synthesis record
sections.what: Holds the complete written conclusions of a run: the executive summary, pillar profiles, case summaries, cross-case comparisons, learning-system notes, and a count of dropped claims.
sections.why: Likely reason: one object holds all the report prose so it can be saved and displayed together.
sections.watch_out: The dropped claim count shows how many statements were removed for weak citations, so a high number means the written text was poorly supported.

sections.name: CaseStance, PillarCited
sections.title: Case stance and pillar citation
sections.what: Defines the four stance labels for how a selected project did in a pillar (strength, weakness, mixed, insufficient), and a cited statement tied to one pillar.
sections.why: The comment states that a stance without a valid citation is stored as insufficient.
sections.watch_out: Insufficient is the safe default, so an unclear result usually means the model could not support a judgement, not that the project was fine.

sections.name: CaseStudy, FailureMode, RecipePractice
sections.title: Case study, failure mode and practice records
sections.what: Describes one full case study, with its group, selection basis, recorded performance, headline, outcome, context, pillar stances, what worked, what went wrong and a timeline. Also defines a failure mode (what went wrong and its effect) and a recipe practice (what to do).
sections.why: The comment says featured cases get a two-page profile, and the failure modes and practices are kept as reusable lessons.
sections.watch_out: Performance is either a recorded value or the words not recorded, so a missing cost must not be read as zero.

sections.name: PillarLesson
sections.title: Lessons for one pillar
sections.what: Gathers the lessons for one pillar: a headline, the single factor that most separates success from trouble, the practices, and the failure modes.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives each pillar a summary section for the lessons part of the report.
sections.watch_out: The differentiator can be empty, so code that displays it must handle the missing case.

sections.name: CaseAnalysis
sections.title: Full case analysis
sections.what: Packs the case studies, pillar lessons, selection details and dropped-claim count for the whole analysis, including how many success and cautionary projects were in the pool.
sections.why: Likely reason: records how cases were chosen so the selection can be explained later.
sections.watch_out: The selection rule is stored as plain text only, so reading it does not repeat the selection.

sections.name: TraceLine
sections.title: Progress trace line
sections.what: Defines one line of a run's progress log: the time since the stage started, its kind (step, read, code, result or warning), and its text.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets someone follow what a long analysis did while it ran.
sections.watch_out: The time resets for each stage, so times cannot be compared directly across stages.

sections.name: RecipeV3Result
sections.title: Whole recipe-v3 result
sections.what: Defines the complete saved output of a v3 run: engine name, time, scope, projects, facts, findings, commentary, methodology, framework, assessment, synthesis, optional case analysis, scene deck flag, totals and slide deck.
sections.why: Likely reason: one saved object lets slides and exports be rebuilt without running the analysis again.
sections.watch_out: The engine name must be recipe-v3 for this shape, and older runs use a different result shape that will not match.

summary: Defines the data shapes for a Lessons Learnt run using the recipe v3 method, so every stage saves and reads the same structure.
purpose: Gives one agreed description of projects, facts, findings, methods, pillars, assessments, synthesis and the final result, so each stage knows what it can rely on.
why: The file header says the method was ported from an earlier skill, and that each fact is checked against its source and project before it can support a driver. These shapes make those rules visible. Beyond that, the reason for each field is not stated in the code.
how: The file contains only type definitions and no running code. It defines the outcome labels, then verification and relevance labels, then records for projects, facts, findings and commentary, then method sources and items, then pillars and sub-drivers, the assessment grid, the synthesis, the case studies and lessons, the progress trace, and finally the complete v3 result.
inputs: Nothing at run time. Other code reads these shapes when it creates or checks data.
outputs: No output of its own. The compiler uses these shapes to flag mismatches in other files.
risks: Changing a field name or making a field required can break saved data and the code that reads it. Several fields are optional because older runs did not store them.
debug: When a type error appears, find the type named in the error and compare its fields with the code that writes that data. For saved runs missing a field, check whether the field is marked optional. Check the engine value on a stored result to see which version produced it.
